                                          PUC PROJECT NO. 58481


    RULEMAKING    TO   IMPLEMENT                            §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                              §
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                           §                     OF TEXAS



    SATOSHI ENERGY COMMENTS ON STAFF'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION ON
        PROJECT NO. 58481, RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD
             INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561


                                               1.​ INTRODUCTION


           Satoshi Energy develops colocated renewable energy and data center infrastructure across

ERCOT and other markets. By partnering closely with both generation asset owners and data

center operators, the company provides a comprehensive approach to interconnection planning

and execution of large load projects. Satoshi Energy has energized 476 megawatts (MW) of data

center facilities colocated with existing renewable generation assets in ERCOT, which comprises

nearly 10% of all large loads energized in ERCOT as of 2025.1 The company is actively

advancing an additional 5 gigawatts (GW) in its ERCOT pipeline. This scale of experience

positions Satoshi Energy as an industry leader of net metering arrangements at scale, bringing

investment, innovation, and high-quality infrastructure to Texas while supporting ERCOT

reliability and economic growth.


           Satoshi Energy appreciates the Commission’s continued efforts to implement PURA

§37.0561 and establish a durable framework for Large Load Interconnection Studies (LLIS). We

support the Commission’s dual mandate to deter speculative load requests while protecting

ratepayers from stranded transmission costs. At the same time, we are concerned that the current
1
    ERCOT. (2025). (rep.). Large Load Interconnection Status Update. Retrieved 2025,.
 structure of financial commitments with insufficient refundability, may unintentionally hinder

viable projects, distort market participation, and slow capital deployment in Texas. These

comments focus on ensuring that financial requirements are proportionate, staged, and aligned

with actual system risk, while preserving the Commission’s objectives of encouraging serious

participation and maintaining grid reliability.



​

                        1.​ COMMENTS ON PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194


General Comments


       Overall, Satoshi Energy recommends a framework in which developers post a

$25,000/MW deposit to initiate studies, receive study results that determine CIAC costs, and

then make a final, non-refundable commitment scaled to CIAC. Importantly, if a load withdraws

prior to the execution of an Interconnection Agreement, they should not be taxed 80% of the

deposit that has yet to be used by TSPs for procuring equipment or performing network

upgrades. This approach balances the need to confirm serious development intent with the

practical reality that developers require information about system capacity and interconnection

costs before committing substantial capital. We outline our proposals in the following two

sections.


Comments on Section (f) Intermediate Agreement


       Satoshi Energy recommends revising the Intermediate Agreement financial security

requirement to $25,000 per MW, with the deposit fully refundable, less actual study or
 procurement costs incurred. The current $50,000/MW requirement imposes substantial capital

commitments before developers receive any planning study results or visibility into system

capacity, upgrade requirements, or interconnection costs. At this stage, developers are effectively

being asked to take on significant financial risk without the ability to make informed decisions.

A $25,000/MW deposit is sufficient to demonstrate serious development intent and ensure that

customers have access to capital, while avoiding unnecessary barriers to entry.


       For example, under the current proposal, a developer submitting 1 GW total across

projects would be required to pay a $40M tax and post a $10M refundable deposit. If the

developer receives unfavorable load results due to limited capacity or outsized transmission

upgrade costs, they would effectively be taxed $40M just to submit a load request and then

withdraw about 6 months later after receiving a result that makes the project unviable.

Refundability of this Intermediate Agreement deposit is critical, regardless of the final

amount that the Commission determines. A financial security at this stage should not function as

a tax for projects that do not move forward based on study results. As a practical matter, a

meaningful portion of projects in each Batch will be withdrawn due to unfavorable outcomes.

Under the current structure, this results in substantial unrecoverable costs that are not tied to any

actual system investment. In other ISOs, initial deposits become non-refundable only at

significant interconnection milestones where the developer has more information on upgrade

costs and schedule to proceed. We encourage the Commission to consider comparable concepts

as to not create an unduly burden on customers looking to develop in Texas


       This issue is particularly acute for loads colocated with generation. The core of Satoshi

Energy’s business model, along with other early market participants, has been the intentional

siting of load at locations that leverage existing generation and transmission infrastructure,
 avoiding the need for system upgrades. Satoshi Energy currently has nearly 2 GW of load studies

completed across multiple TSPs, all with $0 CIAC, reflecting a deliberate strategy to minimize

system impact and decrease risk to ratepayers. Applying uniform financial requirements that do

not account for these differences may discourage precisely the types of projects that most

efficiently utilize existing infrastructure and minimize stranded asset risk. The purpose of the

Intermediate Agreement deposit is to ensure seriousness and enable studies, not to recover

transmission costs. A lower, fully refundable deposit achieves this objective while allowing

developers to obtain study results and make informed decisions before committing additional

capital.


           The current structure also risks unintended market consequences. Developers,

particularly smaller and mid-sized firms, do not have access to unlimited capital. Excessive

upfront requirements may drive consolidation toward larger entities with lower costs of capital,

shifting competition away from project quality and system efficiency.


Comments on Section (i) Interconnection Agreement


           Satoshi Energy recommends eliminating the $50,000/MW interconnection fee and

instead relying solely on a CIAC as the financial obligation at the Interconnection Agreement

stage. At this point of the development process, a developer has more information on load

capacity and ramp schedule from ERCOT, and can make an informed decision whether to move

forward and give the TSPs a green light to securitize long lead-time equipment. At this point, the

initial deposit should be trued up and the unused portions released, except to the extent necessary

to secure long lead-time equipment or services. Once the actual cost of interconnection has been

fully identified and securitized, retaining additional capital does not serve a purpose for TSPs or
 ratepayers alike. This system ensures that financial commitments are directly tied to actual

system costs and project maturity.


       CIAC is an established and effective mechanism that ensures ratepayers are held

harmless by requiring large load customers to pay the full cost of facilities directly attributable to

their interconnection. Because CIAC reflects real system costs, it is the appropriate basis for

financial commitments at this stage. Imposing an additional flat $50,000/MW fee is not tied to

system impact and results in duplicative financial requirements. As mentioned above, this issue

is particularly significant for colocated projects that do not require transmission upgrades. For

these projects, CIAC may be minimal or zero. Requiring a large additional interconnection fee is

not supported by cost causation principles and may significantly exceed the actual cost of

interconnection by tens or hundreds of millions.


       Satoshi Energy agrees the financial commitments should benon-refundable at this stage,

but those commitments should be scaled to CIAC, which reflects actual system impact. This

approach ensures that developers bear full responsibility for required infrastructure without

imposing unnecessary additional costs. Satoshi Energy further recommends allowing CIAC and

related financial obligations to be satisfied through cash, letters of credit, or parental guarantees,

which are standard in infrastructure development and provide equivalent protection while

allowing more efficient capital deployment.
 Conclusion


       Satoshi Energy appreciates the Commission’s continued consideration of these important

issues and its efforts to establish a framework that deters speculative requests while protecting

ratepayers. We respectfully urge the Commission to adopt a final rule that aligns financial

commitments with project maturity and actual system impact, including a $25,000/MW

refundable deposit at the Intermediate Agreement stage and reliance on CIAC as the sole

financial obligation at the Interconnection Agreement stage. A balanced, cost-based approach

will ensure that capital is deployed efficiently, preserve competitive market participation, and

continue to support responsible business development and reliable load growth in ERCOT.




Dated: April 16, 2026


                                     Respectfully submitted,

LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §                   OF TEXAS


      SATOSHI ENERGY EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ON PROJECT NO. 58481

 ●​ The Commission should allow full refundability of Intermediate Agreement
    deposits, less actual costs incurred by ERCOT and TSPs above the study fee. Limiting
    refunds to 20% imposes significant unrecoverable costs that are not tied to any actual
    transmission investment that risk making a project unviable.
 ●​ If a developer submits 1 GW total across projects, it would be required to source $50
    million upfront at the Intermediate Agreement just to enter the queue. If the customer
    then receives unfavorable load results (load cannot be served until 5+ years down the
    line, they would receive a 20% refund of $10M and effectively be taxed $40M penalty
    just to learn a load result that is unworkable for the ILLE. This tax does not align
    with the goal set forth in SB 6 of promoting business development in Texas while
    protecting ratepayers and maintaining system reliability.
 ●​ Satoshi Energy recommends a $25,000/MW deposit at the Intermediate Agreement
    stage. This level is sufficient to demonstrate serious development intent and enable
    studies, while avoiding excessive upfront capital requirements before developers receive
    planning study results or visibility into system impacts. A larger deposit will just increase
    costs going to banks annually, deterring development from coming to Texas and goes
    against the goals laid out in SB 6.
 ●​ Satoshi Energy recommends scaling the fee at the Interconnection Agreement to
    actual Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) costs as the financial obligation
    at the Interconnection Agreement stage. This ensures that the fee collected reflects the
    actual cost of transmission facilities required to serve the load and ensures that ratepayers
    are fully protected without imposing duplicative or unnecessary financial requirements.
 ●​ After CIAC has been determined, any additional Intermediate Agreement deposits should
    be trued up, and unused portions should be refunded. Once interconnection costs are
    identified and securitized through CIAC, retaining additional financial security serves no
    further purpose and increases the cost of capital.
 ●​ Satoshi Energy recommends a risk-based, staged framework aligned with project
    maturity that pairs a moderate, refundable deposit with CIAC-based commitments to
    deter speculative requests, protect ratepayers, and support continued infrastructure
    investment in Texas. This mirrors how generation is developed in the state, practices
    across other ISOs, and has a proven track record.
